query: Which method can be used for high-temperature oxidation behaviour and phase stability, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Integrating in situ high‐energy synchrotron X‐ray diffraction equipped with fast detectors and complementary techniques (e.g., simultaneous thermogravimetric or spectroscopic measurements) will enable the simultaneous, real‐time monitoring of high‐temperature oxidation kinetics and phase evolution in advanced alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: High-temperature alloys or ceramics in a single-phase solid-solution state before exposure to oxidizing environments.
generation.intervention: Application of an integrated in situ high-energy synchrotron XRD setup—with fast detectors and a complementary measurement (such as TGA or in situ spectroscopy)—during exposure to high-temperature oxidation conditions.
generation.conditions: High-temperature reactive environments (e.g., temperatures ranging from 750 °C to above 1200 °C) where oxidation and phase transformations can occur dynamically.
generation.structural_mediator: Real-time changes in diffraction patterns (peak shifts, intensity changes, and emergence of new peaks) that reflect oxidation layer formation and phase transformation events.
generation.mechanism: Fast high-energy XRD can capture transient structural changes while complementary techniques quantify oxidation kinetics (e.g., mass change). The simultaneous measurement enables direct correlation between the onset and progression of oxidation with phase stability or transformation events.
generation.predicted_outcome: The integrated method will reveal a synchronized evolution of oxide formation and phase transitions (or stability retention) under high-temperature conditions, offering a more complete picture than separate ex situ analyses.
generation.baseline: Conventional methods where oxidation behaviour and phase transformations are assessed separately (ex situ or with non-integrated in situ approaches), which can miss dynamic correlations.
generation.boundary: The effectiveness may be limited by the time resolution of detectors and the spatial resolution of complementary techniques; integration challenges and limited temperature ranges of the setup could constrain observations.
generation.uncertainty: The precise sensitivity and time resolution necessary to capture very rapid oxidation or subtle phase shifts are not fully established, and there is uncertainty regarding the synchronization fidelity between XRD and complementary measurements.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a high-temperature alloy sample in an oxidation furnace equipped with an integrated in situ high-energy synchrotron XRD setup and simultaneous thermogravimetric analysis. Run a series of experiments at varying temperatures (e.g., 750 °C, 900 °C, and 1200 °C) while continuously recording XRD patterns and mass change data.
measurements: XRD peak position, intensity, and emergence of new peaks over time
Real-time mass gain/loss from TGA indicating oxidation kinetics
Correlation timing between structural changes and mass change
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the integrated measurements do not show a clear, time-correlated association between the initiation and progression of oxidation (as measured by mass changes) and the observed phase transformations (as indicated by XRD), then the hypothesis that the integrated in situ method effectively captures simultaneous oxidation behavior and phase stability must be rejected.

4.1. Phase Stability at High Temperature

HEAs produced on casting when exposed to long-term annealing cause decomposition into the traditional multi-phase microstructure. The alloys decomposition on annealing at a higher temperature creates doubt about its applicability for high-temperature application (over 800 °C). Thermodynamic calculations were performed to understand whether the solid solution established when cast is a thermodynamically stable phase at potential use temperatures. Phase equilibria of CrMnFeCoNi alloy are visualized in Figure 9 as a one-dimensional step diagram of phase fractions and a function of temperature. From Figure 9 the critical features of phase equilibria are readily discernible, such as the thickness of the HEA’s single-phase FCC region (solvus to the solidus) at high temperature from solidus at 1320 °C down to about 750 °C. Also, it shows the lower temperature decomposition products stated in some works. At a lower temperature, phase equilibria show the formation of the sigma phase and BCC phase.

decision.trend: Earlier studies predominantly analyzed oxidation and phase transformations separately—often using ex situ techniques where oxidation kinetics were inferred post-exposure and phase changes were characterized independently (e.g., by TEM or conventional XRD). Over time, researchers have shifted to performing in situ high-temperature X-ray diffraction (HTXRD) to capture real‐time phase evolution during oxidation. This approach was effectively demonstrated in studies on CrMnFeCoNi high‐entropy alloy, which tracked the transition from MnO to mixed spinel phases while monitoring the phase stability across a broad temperature range.
decision.unsolved: Despite progress, a single measurement tool that simultaneously provides high-resolution, time‐resolved data on both oxidation kinetics and phase transformations remains elusive, especially under dynamic high-temperature conditions in reactive environments.
decision.lever: Developing and applying in situ high-energy synchrotron X-ray diffraction integrated with fast detectors and complementary techniques (such as simultaneous thermogravimetric or spectroscopic measurements) to monitor oxidation kinetics and phase stability in real time
decision.why: This lever builds directly on the trend towards real-time, in situ analysis by enhancing time resolution and data richness. It addresses the current gap by combining methods to capture both the oxidation behavior and phase transformations in a single experiment, which is critical for fully understanding high-temperature performance.
